discovery: Squeezed states of light and their use to beat the standard quantum limit in precision interferometry
motivation: Quantum mechanics sets a noise floor on every optical measurement. In 1981 Carlton Caves showed that this shot-noise limit in interferometers comes from vacuum fluctuations entering the unused port, and that injecting squeezed vacuum could beat it. In 1986 Jeff Kimble's group produced strong squeezing with an optical parametric oscillator, turning a theoretical idea into a practical quantum resource. Roman Schnabel developed squeezed-light sources that are stable, broadband and work at audio frequencies, and in 2010 he put the first one into a gravitational-wave observatory, GEO600. Squeezing now runs routinely in LIGO and Virgo. It increases the rate of detected black-hole and neutron-star mergers and has started to reduce quantum back-action as well. Squeezing has also found uses in quantum sensing, metrology and continuous-variable quantum information. Together, this work turned the quantum vacuum from a fundamental limit into a tool engineers can use.
